extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geologists, and scientifically-minded general readers interested in field natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for conducting and reporting field natural-history and geological observations (collection, measurement, comparative reasoning, and hypothesis evaluation) based on voyages and island studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful empirical observation and vivid description
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce detailed, sensory descriptions of places, organisms, and phenomena (e.g., lagoon colour, coral-fields, behaviour of birds and crabs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly exemplifies long, precise descriptions: 'The shallow, clear, and still water of the lagoon...is of the most vivid green.' Such descriptive passages serve both to record observations and to convey the scene to readers; include visual, tactile, and behavioural details where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive specimen collection and cataloguing
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and record specimens systematically, reporting counts and composition of local flora and fauna (Darwin: 'in my collection...there are twenty species...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record numbers and taxonomic information where possible (plants: 'twenty species'; insects: 'thirteen species'). Note uncertain items (e.g., species heard of but not seen) and separate introduced/ imported species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external authorities and personal communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Corroborate and augment field observations with information from other naturalists, captains, and residents (e.g., 'I must express my obligation to Sir T. Mitchell' ; Mr. Liesk; Professor Henslow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite local residents and published travellers to support or contrast your observations; explicitly state when information is second-hand and the informant's provenance or experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic measurements and simple experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Make and report measurements and field tests (soundings, digging wells, examining lead impressions) to support inferences about limits and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'numerous soundings...within ten fathoms, the prepared tallow...came up marked with the impression of living corals.' Use repeatable techniques (soundings, depth measures) and report method and results to justify conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving inference from organismal ecological limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use known physiological/ecological limits of organisms (e.g., depth limits of reef-building corals) as constraints for geological inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin reasons: 'the utmost depth at which corals can construct reefs is between 20 and 30 fathoms' and uses this to argue that reef foundations must have subsided. Explicitly state biological limits and show how they constrain larger-scale processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit consideration and evaluation of alternative hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: State competing explanations and evaluate them against observed evidence (e.g., crater theory, corals building rings for protection, subsidence theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out alternative theories and explain why some are implausible: Darwin rejects the crater-theory and the 'corals build rings for protection' idea by pointing to size, form, species distributions, and absence of corroborating mechanism. Show which observations favour or disprove each hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of large-scale distributional and comparative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use geographic extent, patterns, and comparisons across archipelagoes to support or refute geological processes ('enormous areas...in which every single island is of coral formation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report ranges, axes, and patterns (e.g., thousands of miles of coral islands) and argue how these distributions make certain formation mechanisms improbable. Comparative examples (Keeling vs Radack vs Maldiva) strengthen inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and investigate anomalous observations; propose plausible transport mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Document anomalies (e.g., a greenstone fragment embedded in calcareous island) and suggest credible mechanisms (transport in roots of a floating tree) rather than ignoring them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the anomaly, consider probabilities of different transport routes, cite analogous cases (Chamisso's Radack observations), and avoid forcing an explanation—present as probable or possible with reasoning about chance events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate local testimony and ethnographic observation cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate statements about local practices, animal uses, and folklore (e.g., Malay spoon spirit dance; reports of drift seeds and canoes) while noting their character and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish careful observation from hearsay; when using local testimony (Mr. Keating, Mr. Liesk), indicate duration of residence and any corroboration. Use such testimony as leads for further investigation rather than definitive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reporting and use of specific figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete numerical details—depths, distances, species counts, dimensional measures—to ground arguments ('no bottom with a line 7200 feet in length...saucer-shaped summit is nearly ten miles across').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, give numeric measures (fathoms, miles, counts) and describe measurement methods so readers can assess scale and precision; avoid vague language when data are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative method across regions and taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare similar ecological or geological phenomena across regions and taxa to identify recurring patterns (e.g., flora and fauna of Keeling resemble those of Radack).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List shared species, functional similarities, and common structural features across sites; use such comparisons to infer common processes or dispersal mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe behaviour and functional morphology to infer adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Record behaviours and structural adaptations that reveal ecological relationships (e.g., Birgos crab tearing and hammering coconut; Scarus fish feeding on coral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe behavioural sequence and relevant morphological traits and discuss how structure and behaviour relate to ecological role or evolutionary adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious, probabilistic language and acknowledgement of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrase conclusions with appropriate caution ('it is improbable', 'I came to the conclusion', 'seems to have been owing') and acknowledge limits of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-assertion; present the strength of evidence and use qualifying language when mechanisms remain speculative. Offer degree of confidence and possible alternative interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis of multi-disciplinary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine biological, geological, and oceanographic data (species distributions, coral physiology, soundings, currents) to build coherent explanations of formation and change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly link observations from different domains (e.g., coral depth limits + soundings + geographic distribution) to support a unified hypothesis (Darwin's subsidence model of atoll formation).
